dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is four days old, and Mike, you're off work today to help Kelly at home, which is exactly where the day should be spent. Overnight, the Ukraine aid-centre death toll rose to 42 ahead of next week's Abu Dhabi peace talks, oil fell for a fourth straight day on hopes the midterm result pushes Washington toward an Iran deal, and the post-election map settled: Democrats hold both chambers of Congress, and Ohio has a governor-elect in Amy Acton and a returning senator in Sherrod Brown. The Cavs lost the rematch in Oklahoma City last night, 124-116, despite Donovan Mitchell's late flurry, and Jarrett Allen left early with a knee knock — they're home Friday against Philadelphia and Saturday against the Knicks. Solon stays cloudy and dry today with a high near 61°, but rain and a sharp cooldown arrive Friday into Saturday, so today is the day for any errands. If energy somehow allows tonight, Hadestown is at Playhouse Square at 7:30 PM.

Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre rises to 42
items.summary:
The death toll from Monday's Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, rose to 42 on Thursday, police said — one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. Up to 33 people were still believed to be buried under the rubble, with rescue and identification work continuing.

Verified bodycam footage from one of the police officers killed showed the moments before a second strike destroyed a shelter where residents were hiding after a radio warning. Ukraine's national police said the attack included a 3-ton glide bomb carrying roughly 1.4 tons of explosives. Russia's Defence Ministry said the strike targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.

The rising toll lands five days before the United States brings Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi. A strike this lethal on people collecting aid hardens Kyiv's negotiating position and raises the pressure on Moscow to show it is serious about a ceasefire.

Watch the Abu Dhabi talks on November 10-11, and whether the Komyshuvakha toll climbs further as rescuers reach the rest of the rubble.

items.title: U.S. to bring Ukraine and Russia together in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11
items.summary:
The United States will bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 to discuss ending the war, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said. The agenda, as Witkoff described it, covers post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and ending the fighting itself.

Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to lead the U.S. side, and the Kremlin has confirmed that Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to President Putin, will be Moscow's chief negotiator. Putin agreed to the new round after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg two weeks ago. The last U.S.-mediated talks were in February, before the U.S. and Israel launched the war against Iran. This week, U.S. negotiators are also meeting European and NATO partners in Brussels on security guarantees and reconstruction support for Ukraine.

Hosting the talks in the Gulf, with both delegations at the same table, is the most structured attempt at an endgame in months. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, hosting President Zelenskiy in Berlin, said Russia must show at Abu Dhabi that it is serious about a ceasefire, and Zelenskiy said he hopes the new Democratic Congress will mean more help for Kyiv.

Watch for the delegations' opening positions early next week — an 'energy ceasefire' and a Black Sea truce to protect food exports are among the first items Zelenskiy wants discussed.

items.title: Netanyahu's position weakens as ultra-Orthodox party withholds support
items.summary:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's fight to stay in power weakened on Thursday after the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism, a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate to form Israel's next government, while an Arab-led party endorsed his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

Israel's October 27 election ended in deadlock. Netanyahu's Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 of 120, but his wider religious-nationalist bloc reached only 53 seats. Eisenkot's coalition won 48, and two parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19. President Isaac Herzog was meeting both men on Thursday night and has until November 11 to pick who gets the first chance to build a coalition; Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister meanwhile.

Netanyahu has seized on an official investigation into possible vote tampering to question the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics call that an attempt to undermine a loss; the Central Election Committee said Wednesday the election's integrity was not compromised.

Watch Herzog's choice by November 11 — and whether the parties that refused to commit on Thursday become kingmakers or force yet another election.

items.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 more years in jail
items.summary:
Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced on Thursday to 10 more years in prison after pleading guilty to colluding with foreign entities under the city's national security law. Wong, who has been behind bars since 2020, will be 40 years old when he leaves jail.

Wong first made headlines at 14, co-founding the student group Scholarism, whose protests forced the government to shelve a pro-China national education plan. By 17 he was the international face of the Umbrella Movement. Prosecutors accused him of working with others between July and November 2020 to solicit foreign sanctions or hostile actions against Hong Kong and China.

The sentence is the latest measure of how completely Beijing's 2020 National Security Law — imposed after the mass protests of 2019 — has reshaped Hong Kong. Activities Wong and his peers once took for granted are now crimes, and the law's cases keep reaching back to the protest era.

The new term runs concurrently with his existing sentence, effectively shortening it by two months, and keeps him in prison past his current release date in January. Wong stood silent in the dock as the judge sentenced him.

items.title: South Korean audit reveals friction in the U.S. alliance
items.summary:
A month-long parliamentary audit in South Korea has surfaced unusual public friction in the alliance with Washington, and President Lee Jae Myung is taking opposition fire over how he has managed the relationship. The strains run from intelligence sharing to White House access and U.S. visa denials for visiting lawmakers.

During the audit, spy chief Lee Jong-seok acknowledged that Washington had curtailed some sensitive intelligence sharing after accusing a South Korean minister of publicly disclosing the location of a previously unconfirmed North Korean nuclear site. South Korea's ambassador to the U.S. raised concerns about limited access to key White House officials. A Pew survey in August found 55% of South Koreans held an unfavourable view of the U.S., the highest in more than 20 years.

Underneath the friction is a shift in Washington's military priorities toward China. U.S. officials say the 28,500 troops in South Korea will stay focused on deterring North Korea, but they have signalled more 'flexibility' to operate beyond the peninsula, potentially including a Taiwan conflict — a prospect that makes Seoul nervous.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Thursday she did not expect major changes after the U.S. midterms, and the defence minister denied any differences to resolve after meeting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Watch whether the intelligence-sharing limits get quietly restored.

items.title: After midterm defeat, Trump faces a stark choice on Iran: deal or escalation
items.summary:
President Trump went to war seeking regime change in Iran. Instead, voters weary of the fighting and hit by soaring fuel prices handed Congress to the Democrats — and Trump now faces a stark choice between cutting a deal with Tehran and escalating a war he cannot easily sustain politically.

The war began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on February 28 and spread across the region as Tehran fired missiles and drones at Gulf targets and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The campaign badly damaged Iran's military but left its nuclear programme unresolved. Two sources close to Gulf government circles told Reuters that a weakened Trump, facing a Congress that can constrain his military options, now has a greater incentive to deal, and a full-scale assault looks less likely.

Tehran is not softening: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned against 'even the slightest inclination towards submission,' and two senior Iranian sources said Tehran stays on high alert, fearing Trump might answer defeat with a strike. Gulf states, for their part, want any settlement to protect freedom of navigation through Hormuz.

Reuters flags one middle path — further limited strikes on nuclear facilities that let Washington claim its objectives were met — while China steps up efforts to broker a settlement. Watch Qatar's mediation and any signal from Tehran in the coming days.

items.title: Democrats ride anti-Trump wave to win control of Congress
items.summary:
Democrats have captured both chambers of Congress, pushing deep into traditionally Republican territory to flip states and districts that President Trump carried. Decision Desk HQ and NBC projected a Democratic Senate after the House had already been called earlier on election night, and the Associated Press later confirmed the House result as well.

Democrats needed four seats to take the Senate and flipped six — in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa. Adam Hamilton is projected to be the first Democrat to win a Kansas Senate seat since 1932, and James Talarico the first in Texas since 1988. Republicans entered the night holding 53 Senate seats and favoured to keep the chamber.

The sweep marks a clear rebuke of the president, who barnstormed the country in the final weeks without holding the red states. Cost of living and the Iran war ran through the results, and the new majority takes power in January with committee gavels and subpoena power.

Watch the organising fights now: Hakeem Jeffries is bidding for speaker, and House Republicans are choosing a new leader after Mike Johnson stepped aside.

items.title: Vance repudiates the Iran war after the electoral defeat
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance distanced himself from President Trump's war on Iran on Wednesday, questioning its worth and blaming it entirely for the defeat that delivered Congress to the Democrats. 'The reason we lost is the war,' Vance wrote on X, adding that anyone who thought losing the Senate for six years was worth it should say so.

Vance also said an earlier recommendation to end the war had been 'sound advice.' He played down any split with Trump, noting the president had acknowledged the war cost Republicans too — though Trump's own comments were more measured, and he told the Wall Street Journal of the war: 'I did the right thing' and 'I would have done it again.'

A sitting vice president publicly second-guessing the president's central military decision is rare, and it lands just as Trump weighs whether to restart major combat operations against Iran — a step U.S. officials told Reuters is still under consideration.

Reuters notes the remarks also raise questions about senior Pentagon officials, notably Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is deeply unpopular in the incoming Congress, where some lawmakers are expected to seek his impeachment.

items.title: Jeffries launches his bid to become the first Black House speaker
items.summary:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries formally launched his bid for speaker on Wednesday in a letter to colleagues obtained by Axios. 'I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives,' the letter opens; if elected, the New York Democrat would be the 57th speaker and the first Black speaker in American history.

Jeffries organised his pitch around three priorities — 'Affordability,' 'Accountability' and 'American Values.' His first-100-days programme, as reported from the letter, includes reversing Medicaid cuts, restoring SNAP funding, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicating the Trump tariffs and stopping the war in Iran.

Jeffries posted late Wednesday that House Democrats are on track to win at least 255 seats, a working majority with room to spare. He would take the gavel from Republican Mike Johnson, who said this week he will not seek the minority leader post.

The full House votes for speaker on January 3, when the new Congress convenes — the first real test of whether Jeffries' majority holds together.

items.title: Johnson steps aside, setting up a House GOP leadership fight between Scalise and Jordan
items.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff on Wednesday that he will not seek to lead House Republicans in the next Congress, after the party lost its majority in Tuesday's midterms. Johnson announced the decision on a morning staff call, according to two sources cited by CNN, after discussing it with President Trump.

The move reverses Johnson's pre-election position: in October he told CBS News he intended to stay on as the top House Republican even if the party lost the majority. Trump had endorsed Johnson's reelection on Monday, calling him 'a true friend, fighter, and WINNER.'

Two heavyweights moved quickly. Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio announced his run to lead House Republicans in the minority in a letter to colleagues, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana was also expected to announce his candidacy on Wednesday.

The secret-ballot leadership elections are expected next week. Whoever wins inherits a minority party arguing in public — including over the vice president's claim that the Iran war cost them the election.

items.title: Democrats flip five governorships — Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada
items.summary:
Democrats flipped five Republican-held governors' offices on Tuesday, all in states President Trump carried in 2024, giving the party an advantage in the nationwide gubernatorial count for the first time in more than a decade. Republicans entered Election Day holding 26 governorships to Democrats' 24; with two races still uncalled, Democrats had secured at least 28.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office; the AP called the race late Tuesday at roughly 53.8% to 44.9%. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms beat Rick Jackson by about 54.3% to 45.7% after eight years under term-limited Brian Kemp, and reporting notes she becomes the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history.

Iowa's Rob Sand broke a decade of GOP control of state government, Nevada's Aaron Ford beat Governor Joe Lombardo with about 51.7%, and in Ohio, Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy 52.3% to 44.4% in the open race.

Governors matter most where Congress cannot reach: redistricting, election administration and state-level responses to federal policy will now run through Democratic statehouses in several former Republican strongholds.

items.title: AI selloff extends globally as Dow futures rise after midterm sweep
items.summary:
Artificial-intelligence stocks kept weakening around the world on Thursday as investors absorbed the Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterms. Dow futures rose 0.4%, pointing to more gains after Wednesday's post-election surge, but Nasdaq futures fell 0.7% and S&P 500 futures were flat, with chip and data-centre shares under pressure.

The split has a political logic: strategists expect Democratic wins in Congress and in governor's races — particularly in Texas — to slow the build-out of data centres, a theme voters themselves endorsed in dozens of local ballot measures. UBS strategists said a slowdown 'should impact estimates for AI infrastructure stocks as well as cloud companies.' In South Korea, Samsung Electronics fell 7.5% and SK Hynix 9.5%, and the selling spread across Japan and Europe.

For perspective, Wednesday itself was a rally for the history books: the Dow's best day since April 2025 and its strongest post-midterms performance since 1982. Oil held below $100, Treasury yields fell to eight-week lows, gold moved back above $4,100 and Bitcoin topped $80,000.

Ahead today: a Bank of England rate decision markets see as a likely quarter-point hike, and earnings from ConocoPhillips and Sony.

items.title: Oil falls for a fourth straight day as midterm result raises hopes of an Iran deal
items.summary:
Oil fell for a fourth consecutive session on Thursday as traders bet the midterm result lowers the odds of further military escalation in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent futures slipped about 1% to $93.65 a barrel and U.S. crude fell about 1.3% to $86.98 in early trading.

The move caps a dramatic week: both benchmarks plunged more than 8% on Wednesday to their lowest levels since August 31. Republicans' loss of Congress raised expectations that a Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain President Trump's military options and push toward a deal with Iran, and two sources close to Gulf governments told Reuters a full-scale assault now looks less likely.

The fundamentals have shifted too. Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near pre-war levels, and JPMorgan says resumed Gulf supplies have pushed the global market back into surplus after months of disruption. Qatar has stepped up mediation between Washington and Tehran.

The deal itself is not close: a senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides remain far apart, and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has signalled U.S. hostility will persist whoever controls Congress. Watch whether prices hold the $90 line if talks stall.

items.title: OpenAI to buy Pierre Computer and fold its code storage into Codex
items.summary:
OpenAI said on November 4 that it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, a San Francisco developer-tools startup whose Git-based Code Storage service lets apps and AI agents store code and its history. Financial terms were not disclosed, the deal needs regulatory approval, and the companies stay separate until it closes.

This is less an acquisition of strangers than a formalising of an existing dependency: Pierre's open-source Trees and Diffs libraries already power file browsing and code review inside OpenAI's Codex app, and Code Storage counts Lovable, Bolt and Amp among its users. OpenAI plans to fold Code Storage into Codex, extending the product from writing code toward storing, reviewing and shipping it. Pierre's open-source projects will remain open.

Axios framed the deal as OpenAI taking aim at Microsoft's GitHub, just as coding agents write more of the world's software and the infrastructure underneath them becomes strategic. Days earlier OpenAI described Pando, its in-house source-control backend, which it says cut median push latency by nearly 80%.

Watch the competitive response: Cursor launched a rival platform, Origin, in August, and Meta bought a coding startup of its own the same day.

items.title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor
items.summary:
Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup whose product lets developers spin up software projects by deploying multiple AI agents into parallel workspaces — each working in an isolated copy of the codebase — then review and merge the results. The deal was first reported by Axios on November 4, and Meta confirmed it to TechCrunch without disclosing terms.

Conductor supports agents including Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex and Cursor, with users paying through their own subscriptions. Founder and CEO Charlie Holtz announced 'Conductor is joining Meta' on Wednesday; he and CTO Jackson de Campos join Meta Superintelligence Labs, working with Nat Friedman and Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang.

The company moved fast and exits fast: founded in 2024 out of Y Combinator, it launched its core product only last summer and raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix Partners.

For existing users, the wind-down is already scheduled — new sign-ups are halted, Conductor Cloud goes read-only on November 13 and shuts down November 20, and core local features run until early 2027. The deal landed the same day OpenAI moved to buy Pierre, underlining how quickly the AI coding stack is consolidating.

items.title: Qualcomm shares slide as smartphone chip sales miss and forecast disappoints
items.summary:
Qualcomm fell short of Wall Street estimates for fourth-quarter smartphone chip sales on Wednesday, and its shares dropped more than 6% in extended trading and about 10% in Thursday premarket trading. Handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion, below the $5.25 billion analysts expected, dragging the chip segment down 8% to $9.02 billion.

The backdrop is a brutal phone market: global smartphone shipments fell 20% in the September quarter to a 14-year low, according to Counterpoint Research, as surging memory-chip costs — driven by AI data-centre demand — pushed device prices up. Declining Apple revenue also weighed, and CEO Cristiano Amon said the current-quarter forecast assumes no further sales to Apple, while adding that Android handset sales have bottomed and are ticking up.

The headline guidance was not all bad: Qualcomm expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of $10.4–$11.2 billion, above the consensus midpoint, and $650 million in data-centre sales, well above the $539 million analysts expected. Automotive chips were a bright spot, with revenue up 89% year over year to about $1.99 billion.

The adjusted profit guide — $2.15 to $2.35 a share, midpoint below estimates — is what investors seized on. Watch whether the data-centre ramp can offset the handset slide.

items.title: Sony profit jumps 45% on Spider-Man and PlayStation, and it raises its outlook
items.summary:
Sony reported a 45% rise in second-quarter operating profit on Thursday, to 622.3 billion yen (about $3.95 billion), beating market estimates on the strength of its games and movies businesses. The company also raised its full-year operating profit outlook by 9%, to about 1.87 trillion yen in one summary of the results.

The hit film 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' helped the movies unit, while PlayStation anchored games. Sony sold 2.6 million PlayStation 5 consoles in the quarter, down from 4 million a year earlier, and it also lifted its outlook for its image-sensor chips and music divisions.

Sony's games business is expected to be a major beneficiary of the launch of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' on November 19, one of the biggest releases in the industry's history.

The pressure point is memory: like every hardware maker, Sony is grappling with higher memory-chip prices caused by the AI boom, though it said in July it had secured the memory it needs to meet this year's projected sales volume.

items.title: Trump says he will accept the midterm results and work with Democrats
items.summary:
President Trump told the New York Times in an election-night phone interview that he is 'absolutely willing' to accept the midterm results, and his message to CBS News was similar: 'Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.' To Politico he added, 'We're gonna work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country, very important.'

At the same time, Trump repeatedly distanced himself from the losses. 'I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!' he posted, and he told Politico, 'They didn't like the candidates in most cases.' He said he had no regrets about endorsing candidates who lost, despite travelling to more than 30 places this fall to try to hold Republican seats.

He also reminded everyone of the leverage he keeps. Trump noted his veto power to the Wall Street Journal — calling the veto the 'ultimate power,' overridable only by two-thirds of Congress — and posted a mockup of his red hat reading 'VETO' on Truth Social. On the Iran war's role in the defeat, he conceded it was 'a piece of it.'

What happens next depends on which Trump shows up: divided government gives both sides reasons to deal on affordability, and equal reasons to fight. The new Congress convenes in January.

items.title: Voters reject data centers in nearly every local ballot measure across 10 states
items.summary:
Amid the national wave, one of Tuesday's clearest verdicts was local: voters overwhelmingly moved to restrict the data-centre boom. Data centres appeared on roughly 45 ballot measures across 10 states, and by early Wednesday at least 33 restriction measures had passed, with trackers later putting the count at about 40 of 41 going the way of tighter limits.

Ohio was the strongest rebuke. The state hosts 257 data centres, they were on the ballot in about 20 communities, and the vote to restrict won or was projected to win everywhere — two localities voted 76% and 77% against allowing data centres nearby. Democrat Sherrod Brown made opposition to data centres the centre of his winning Senate platform in Ohio. Only one town, Harwood, North Dakota, voted down a measure that would have added public-hearing requirements for large industrial projects.

Exit polling suggests this was not a side issue: an NBC exit poll found 56% of voters said AI and data centres played a 'major' or 'crucial' role in their vote. Winning governors in Texas and Georgia both promised pauses on new approvals.

Axios called it an 'AI earthquake.' Strategists estimate moratoriums could put roughly 30% of expected 2028 data-centre capacity at risk — one reason AI infrastructure stocks are sliding this week.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed becomes the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, winning Michigan
items.summary:
Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. The Associated Press called the race at 2:27 a.m. Wednesday, with El-Sayed at about 52.4% of the counted vote to Rogers' 45.6%.

El-Sayed, 42, is a physician and epidemiologist who served as a Detroit and county health official. Born in Rochester Hills to Egyptian immigrant parents and raised in the Detroit area, he ran on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and reducing corporate influence in politics. He told AP that Michigan had rejected a 'hateful, spiteful campaign' after months of Republican criticism.

He replaces outgoing Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat not seeking reelection, in a seat Democrats have held since 1979. Rogers, 63, is a former U.S. representative.

El-Sayed's win headlined a night of historic firsts in CNN's roundup of the 2026 results. He takes office with the new Senate in January, in a chamber his party now controls.

items.title: Xavier Becerra wins California governor's race, becoming the state's first elected Latino governor
items.summary:
Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's next governor. The Associated Press declared him the winner shortly after polls closed on Tuesday, and with about half the expected vote counted he led Republican Steve Hilton by 64.2% to 35.8% — a margin of more than 1.6 million votes.

Becerra, 68, will be the first Latino elected governor of California; the last Latino to hold the office, Romualdo Pacheco in 1875, was elevated from lieutenant governor a century and a half ago. He succeeds term-limited Gavin Newsom and is due to be sworn in on January 4, 2027, extending Democrats' hold on the state's top office.

His résumé runs through every level of Democratic politics: U.S. congressman from Los Angeles, California attorney general, and U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services under President Biden. Hilton, a former Fox News host endorsed by President Trump, never closed the gap.

The win caps an unlikely arc — in March, Becerra was polling so low he faced calls to drop out of a crowded primary. He campaigned in part on a pro-housing platform, and housing affordability will be the first test of his governorship.

items.title: SpaceX picks Qualcomm to build Starlink Mobile's nationwide U.S. 5G network
items.summary:
Qualcomm has signed a multi-year agreement with SpaceX to supply the radio equipment, baseband units and software for Starlink Mobile's planned nationwide terrestrial 5G network, the companies announced Wednesday. Qualcomm called it 'our biggest 5G deal yet'; financial terms were not disclosed.

The equipment — Qualcomm's Dragonwing radio units and distributed-unit processors, using massive MIMO antennas with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths — is slated for deployment across tens of thousands of macro cell sites in the U.S. starting in 2027. Starlink described the project on X as 'the first fully-integrated US nationwide satellite and terrestrial network.'

The terrestrial build complements Starlink's satellite service and follows SpaceX's October agreement to acquire a nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, subject to FCC approval. No live sites, coverage map or prices were published with the announcement.

If it delivers, the network would challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile on their home turf with a satellite company as the new fourth carrier. SpaceX shares slipped more than 1% in Thursday premarket trading, extending recent losses.

items.title: October jobs report lands Friday, with the Fed's December decision in the balance
items.summary:
The October jobs report arrives Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET, and it is the week's biggest economic test. Previews expect payrolls to rise by 50,000 to 65,000 after September's modest gain of 29,000, with unemployment holding at 4.2% and wages rising 0.3% on the month.

The number lands in a tense policy moment. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75–4.00% on October 28 in a 10–2 vote, and markets currently price roughly a 70–78% chance of a December hike — meaning a hot jobs report could firm that up, while a soft one could reopen the case for standing pat. At least three Fed officials, including Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin, speak Thursday ahead of the release.

For households, the stakes are concrete: mortgage and borrowing costs follow the Fed's path, and a labour market that is cooling but not cracking is the narrow path policymakers have been trying to walk all year.

Watch the wage figure as much as the headline — pay growth running hot is the detail most likely to move the December odds.

items.title: Amy Acton beats Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio's first woman elected governor
items.summary:
Democrat Amy Acton won the Ohio governor's race on Tuesday, defeating Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and becoming the first woman elected governor in Ohio history. Later unofficial figures from the Secretary of State put Acton at 52.3% to Ramaswamy's 44.3%, with Libertarian Don Kissick at 3.3%.

Acton, 60, is a physician and Ohio's former health director during COVID who ran as a first-time candidate. She ends Democrats' 20-year losing streak in Ohio governor's races in a state President Trump won three times, campaigning on property and income tax relief, public education and tougher requirements for data centres. The race turned personal late, when a Ramaswamy ad featured Acton's estranged mother and Acton answered by recounting a childhood marked by abuse, neglect and periods of homelessness.

She succeeds term-limited Republican Governor Mike DeWine and promised to govern across party lines: 'I will work with anyone and everyone... to make life better for Ohio.'

She will not face a veto-proof legislature: Democrats broke the Ohio House GOP supermajority on the same night, though Republicans kept theirs in the state Senate. Results stay unofficial until counties certify.

items.title: Sherrod Brown completes comeback, beats Jon Husted to return to the U.S. Senate
items.summary:
Former Senator Sherrod Brown defeated incumbent Senator Jon Husted in Ohio's Senate special election, completing a comeback two years after losing his seat. The AP called the race for Brown; its results table with 98% reporting showed Brown at 2,301,042 votes to Husted's 2,077,748.

Husted was appointed by Governor DeWine in January 2025 to replace JD Vance when Vance became vice president, and this was his first Senate race. Brown's win helps Democrats take control of the U.S. Senate, and he becomes only the seventh former senator since 1946 to lose his seat and later return. Brown hammered Husted over support for data centres and tied their energy demands to rising utility costs; the campaigns and outside groups raised more than $80 million, with total Ohio election spending reported above $517 million.

The special election fills only the remainder of Vance's term, so Brown would have to run again in 2028 for a full six years.

Timing: under state law Husted leaves office December 15, and Brown could be sworn in as early as that date once the vote is certified.

items.title: Clase and Ortiz pitch-rigging trial opens in Brooklyn, prosecutors call them 'cheaters'
items.summary:
Opening statements in the pitch-rigging trial of former Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz began Wednesday in Brooklyn federal court, and prosecutors did not mince words. 'The defendants, Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, are cheaters,' Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola told jurors.

Prosecutors say Clase befriended a sports bettor in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 and began feeding him pitch information, then recruited Ortiz in 2025. Gamblers allegedly won at least $460,000 betting on whether individual pitches would be balls or strikes. The government alleges Clase rigged at least 18 pitches across 17 games between May 2023 and May 2025, often by intentionally throwing balls or tipping off-speed pitches. Both men pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges including wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies; NewsNet5 reports the charges carry up to 65 years if convicted on all counts.

Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time AL Reliever of the Year. Both pitchers were arrested in November 2025, are free on bail, and remain on unpaid, non-disciplinary leave from the Guardians.

Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto is presiding, and the trial is expected to run about three weeks.

items.title: Ohio voters pass Issue 3 voter-ID amendment as Democrats take most statewide offices
items.summary:
Ohio voters overwhelmingly approved Issue 3, writing the state's voter-ID rules into the Ohio Constitution. With 98% reporting, the AP table showed Yes at 2,934,245 votes to No at 1,556,864 — roughly two-to-one support.

The amendment mirrors the existing law requiring photo ID when voting in person. Supporters say it stops future lawmakers from weakening ID rules; critics call it unnecessary, since Ohio already has a photo ID law and little evidence of widespread fraud. Down the ballot, Democrat Allison Russo won secretary of state, becoming Ohio's top elections official, Republican Frank LaRose held the auditor's office, and Democrats John Kulewicz (attorney general) and Seth Walsh (treasurer) led their races in the November 5 roundups.

The Ohio Supreme Court races were close too: Justice Jennifer Brunner and Judge Marilyn Zayas held narrow leads in early counts, and Zayas would be the first Latina on the court if her lead holds. Republicans have held a majority of the court's seven seats since 1986.

All results remain unofficial until county certification; Cuyahoga County's is scheduled for November 24.

items.title: Northeast Ohio flips a House seat and passes Cuyahoga County levies
items.summary:
Northeast Ohio had its own earthquake on Tuesday. Democrat Brian Poindexter unseated Representative Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District — unofficial Secretary of State returns showed Poindexter at 54.9% to Miller's 45.1%, and Miller conceded late Tuesday. Poindexter is an ironworker and Brook Park city council member; the race had turned on abuse allegations by Miller's ex-wife, which he vehemently denied.

Cuyahoga County voters passed both big levies: Issue 10 for developmental disabilities with nearly 63%, and Issue 11 for health and human services with about 60%. Together they add $166.50 a year per $100,000 of property value. Voters also approved Charter Issues 12, 13 and 14, which limit some executive powers, and Democrat Courtney Scheff's win in County Council District 5 leaves the council with no Republicans.

More than 1.7 million Ohioans voted early, a record for a governor's election year. Akron voters approved housing and police-oversight charter amendments, while only about a third of Northeast Ohio school tax increases passed.

County certification is scheduled for November 24, after which the unofficial numbers become final.

items.title: Ohio Democrats take a majority of the state's U.S. House seats and end the state House supermajority
items.summary:
Democrats will control 8 of Ohio's 15 congressional seats after flipping three Republican-held districts under the map approved in 2025 — Brian Poindexter over Max Miller, Kristina Knickerbocker over longtime Representative Mike Turner (49% to 47%), and Don Leonard over Mike Carey (52% to about 45%). Representative Marcy Kaptur held the 9th District with 52%; she has served since 1983 and is the longest-serving woman in Congress.

In Columbus, Democrats declared victory in eight Ohio House seats previously held by Republicans, with recounts possible in four more. That drops the GOP below the 60-seat supermajority it has held since 2013, so the House is no longer veto-proof against Governor-elect Amy Acton. Republicans lost only two state Senate seats and keep their supermajority there.

Analysts quoted by the Dispatch caution that the results look like a referendum on President Trump rather than proof Ohio has become a blue state — Republicans have controlled the Ohio Senate since 1984.

Even so, it was Democrats' best Ohio night since 2006, and it changes the math on everything from budgets to redistricting fights in the new year.

items.title: Federal government rejects Cleveland's $7.8 million lead-safety grant
items.summary:
The federal government has rejected Cleveland's application for a $7.8 million lead-safety grant, after HUD ran a risk review and judged the city too risky to manage the money based on its performance across several federal housing grants. Signal Cleveland's reporting stresses the denial was not about need — Cleveland's lead problem is well documented — but about how the city has handled federal housing money overall.

The city is seeking a debriefing, checking whether it can appeal, and looking for other ways to pay for lead cleanup. Cleveland still has three older HUD lead grants in progress, but all are winding down, and there is no fresh federal lead money lined up to replace them.

For a city where lead paint in older housing remains one of the most serious threats to young children, a gap in funding means fewer homes remediated on schedule — and more pressure on county and state programmes to fill in.

Watch the city's appeal decision and whether Ohio steps in with bridge funding before the older grants run out.

baby.tip: Day 4 tip — diaper math: by today Benji should be having at least 3–4 wet diapers and several stools a day, and the counts should keep climbing toward 6+ wet diapers by day five or six. Keep the little log going on the fridge or phone; it's the simplest feeding check there is, and it's exactly what his pediatrician's office will ask about. If a full day looks low, that's a call-the-pediatrician question, not a wait-and-see one.
baby.fact: At four days old, Benji can only focus clearly on things about 8 to 12 inches from his face — which is, not coincidentally, about the distance to a parent's face during a feeding. High-contrast patterns and your faces are basically his favourite channel right now.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for Day 4: the first tummy-time minute — a short, supervised session on a firm surface while Benji is awake and calm. One minute counts as a win, and a Moose-supervised (from a polite distance) session counts double.
